case_study_insert.main_stem: Xplore Automation (XPL) is a public limited company in the industrial robotics sector, designing warehouse picking robots and computer-vision quality systems for factories in Germany. Founded in 2008 by Stefan Bauer, it employs a workforce of 62 and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, with engineering decisions taken by the technical director. XPL plans to invest $1,200,000 in a robotic picking line with automated optical inspection, financed by $700,000 hire purchase and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. Two problems remain: calibration faults have lifted the weld defect rate to 4.8%, and skilled technician turnover is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: XPL assembled 9,800 robotic cells last quarter, of which 4.8% failed weld inspection, down from 7.3% a year earlier. Client complaints averaged 31 a quarter and 9 of 24 factory customers now require predictive-maintenance evidence before renewing. Mean repair time is 4.1 days and first-pass yield is 96.4%. A survey of 240 production managers found that 71% would pay up to $1.20 more for predictive maintenance, and 63% rank uptime above price. A training review shows 15 of 62 technicians lack computer-vision skills; a technical college course costs $1,100 per technician.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Xplore Automation for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of hire purchase and other borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.49 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across engineering firms. (3) Semiconductor and servo-motor input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while demand for industrial automation grew 4.8% and factory wages overall rose 3.6%.

questions.question_text: XPL plans to finance $700,000 of its $1,200,000 robotic line through hire purchase. Explain two advantages for XPL of using the $500,000 share issue instead.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share issue finance carries no regular hire-purchase instalments, which protects XPL's cash flow while it already has fixed costs of $420,000 a year and pays interest of $78,000. Each instalment avoided can instead fund work on the 4.8% weld defect rate or the 4.1-day mean repair time, protecting the $14.00 contribution per unit and the $26.00 selling price. With the base rate due to rise to 4.75% (Appendix 3), hire-purchase charges would become dearer, whereas equity does not re-price with the market.

Point 2: A share issue does not give a lender security over the $1,200,000 robotic line, so XPL cannot lose the automated optical inspection equipment if automation demand grows more slowly than the 4.8% forecast. It also spreads the funding risk among shareholders rather than committing the public limited company to fixed debt repayments while the 9 of 24 factory customers demand predictive-maintenance evidence before renewal. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders, but that is preferable to a repossession risk on the core production asset.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to XPL's financing, costs and customers.

questions.question_text: XPL is launching a predictive-maintenance service. Consider advertising in a robotics trade magazine, sponsoring an international automation exhibition, or running an engineering influencer campaign on LinkedIn. Which should XPL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Robotics trade magazine advertising: A technical advert can explain predictive maintenance in detail and reaches plant engineers and robotics integrators who specify equipment, including buyers like the 9 of 24 factory customers who now demand evidence before renewal. It can quote the fall in weld defects from 7.3% to 4.8% and the 96.4% first-pass yield. Its readership is limited and print is slow, and it cannot demonstrate the $1,200,000 robotic line in action, which matters when 71% of 240 surveyed managers would pay $1.20 more for predictive maintenance.

International automation exhibition sponsorship: A major exhibition draws thousands of factory decision-makers and gives XPL a stand for live demonstrations of optical inspection, building trust quickly with the 63% who rank uptime above price. It also generates distributor leads in new markets. The costs of stands, travel and staffing are high while XPL is already funding $700,000 of hire purchase, and most visitors are browsers whose orders will not arrive before the year end.

LinkedIn engineering influencer campaign: Respected automation engineers can demonstrate predictive maintenance with real uptime data to a targeted audience of factory managers at a low cost per contact, with every click measurable. The message can address the 4.8% weld defects and the 4.1-day repair time directly. Reach is narrower than an exhibition and credibility depends on the influencer, but the audience is precisely XPL's buyer.

Recommendation: XPL should choose the engineering influencer campaign. It targets the managers in its own research, demonstrates the product and costs far less than an exhibition. The exhibition is rejected as expensive and speculative while $700,000 of hire purchase must be serviced, and the trade magazine is rejected as too passive and slow to prove a $1,200,000 robotic system; XPL should place the best influencer demonstrations in its technical advertising afterwards.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to XPL's robotics market.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some contextual evidence and emerging judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options using XPL's survey data, defect record and financing, with a justified recommendation that explains why the other two are rejected.

questions.question_text: XPL's weld defect rate is 4.8% and technician turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for XPL of autocratic leadership and a hierarchical structure in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets the technical director set one clear quality standard for all 62 staff, which is useful when 4.8% of welds fail inspection and 31 complaints a quarter arrive from customers. Decisions about recalibrating the $1,200,000 robotic line can be made immediately without consulting everyone, so the 96.4% first-pass yield can be protected and the 9 of 24 factory customers kept satisfied while predictive-maintenance evidence is prepared.

Point 2: A hierarchical structure gives a clear chain of command and defined responsibilities, so a calibration fault can be traced to a named technician and corrected through the levels rather than being passed between teams. That helps reduce the 4.1-day mean repair time and supports the 71% of surveyed managers who would pay $1.20 more for predictive maintenance. Clear promotion paths in a hierarchy also give skilled technicians a reason to stay, easing the turnover problem that currently threatens output of 60,000 units a year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to XPL's defect rate, turnover and customer demands.

questions.question_text: XPL must train 15 technicians in computer-vision skills. Consider on-the-job training by the equipment supplier or off-the-job training at a technical college costing $1,100 per technician. Which should XPL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training by the supplier: The supplier's engineers can train the 15 technicians on the actual optical-inspection systems in the $1,200,000 robotic line, so learning matches the exact cameras and fault codes behind the 4.8% weld defect rate. It costs no course fees and keeps all 62 employees productive, which matters while mean repair time is 4.1 days. The weaknesses are that the visit is short, the training is not formally certified, and knowledge stays with a few technicians who may leave as turnover rises.

Off-the-job training at the technical college: The $1,100 per technician course gives structured teaching in computer vision and a recognised qualification for all 15, costing $16,500 in total (15 × $1,100). That is worthwhile against a $1,200,000 investment and helps the 9 of 24 factory customers who want predictive-maintenance evidence. It removes technicians from the factory, however, and generic content must still be adapted to XPL's own robots.

Decision: XPL should choose on-the-job training by the supplier as the main method, with a short college module for the senior technicians who will supervise the system. It is immediate, specific to the installed equipment and keeps skilled staff on the line while 31 complaints a quarter and a 4.8% defect rate demand attention. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 15 technicians would slow the 9,800 cells assembled each quarter and the generic course would not solve the calibration faults; it can be added later once the line is stable. The recognised qualification would also help XPL retain the technicians whose departure is raising costs: recruiting and inducting replacements while 4.8% of welds fail inspection is more expensive than the $16,500 course.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to XPL's skills gap.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in XPL's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensively evaluates both methods against cost, disruption and equipment specificity, with a clear decision and explicit reasons for rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how XPL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data to plan the robotic line.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($26.00 − $12.00) = $420,000 ÷ $14.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate XPL's average total cost per unit.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = Fixed costs ÷ Output + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ 60,000 units = $7.00, plus $12.00 = $19.00. Answer: average total cost is $19.00 a unit.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways XPL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 30,000 units against output of 60,000 units gives a margin of safety of 30,000 units, so XPL can absorb a dip in demand or a rise in the 4.8% defect rate before the robotic line stops covering its $420,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $14.00 lets managers test the $1.20 premium that 71% of 240 surveyed managers would pay for predictive maintenance: adding it to the $26.00 price lifts contribution and reduces the output needed to break even.
3. Average total cost of $19.00 a unit is a benchmark for the $1,200,000 investment: if optical inspection cuts the 4.8% defect rate and the 4.1-day repair time without raising the $12.00 variable cost, unit cost falls and the margin over average cost widens.
4. The 30,000-unit margin of safety also helps judge the $700,000 hire-purchase commitment: managers can check that enough units are sold above break-even to meet instalments before the base rate rises to 4.75%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Average total cost = $19.00 a unit | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 30,000 units against the 4.8% defect rate; testing the $1.20 predictive-maintenance premium; unit-cost benchmarking at $19.00 for the $1,200,000 line; and checking hire-purchase affordability at 4.75% interest.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate XPL's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has XPL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.5%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $2,000,000 ÷ revenue $5,000,000 × 100 = 40.0; 2025 $2,610,000 ÷ $5,800,000 × 100 = 45.0, while cost of sales moved only from $3,000,000 to $3,190,000. Operating profit $500,000 ÷ revenue $5,000,000 × 100 = 10.0 in 2024 and $725,000 ÷ $5,800,000 × 100 = 12.5 in 2025. Returns on capital: $500,000 ÷ $2,500,000 × 100 = 20.0 in 2024 and $725,000 ÷ $2,900,000 × 100 = 25.0 in 2025. Interest payable rose from $60,000 to $78,000 but remained a small share of operating profit.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The gross margin improved from 40.0% to 45.0%, showing tight control of production costs while revenue grew $800,000, helped by the 4.8% growth in automation demand and the 71% of managers willing to pay $1.20 more for predictive maintenance. The operating margin rose from 10.0% to 12.5%, so more of each revenue dollar survives the $420,000 fixed costs. Returns on capital climbed from 20.0% to 25.0% even though capital employed increased by $400,000 and hire purchase of $700,000 is planned, evidence that the existing robotic capacity is being used effectively. The improvement is genuine because revenue and gross profit both grew, not merely because costs were delayed. The caution is that 4.8% of welds still fail, mean repair time is 4.1 days and semiconductor input costs are up 14.2%; these could erode the gains if the new line is badly commissioned.

Conclusion: XPL's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (40.0% to 45.0%), operating margin (10.0% to 12.5%) and returns on capital (20.0% to 25.0%) all rose together with revenue. XPL should protect the position by using part of the $500,000 share issue to cut the 4.8% defect rate and retain technicians before the $1,200,000 line is installed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for XPL of adding automated optical inspection to its robotic picking line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Optical inspection can detect the weld faults behind the 4.8% defect rate immediately, cutting the 31 complaints a quarter and the 4.1-day mean repair time while lifting the 96.4% first-pass yield. That supports the 71% of 240 surveyed managers who would pay $1.20 more for predictive maintenance and the 9 of 24 factory customers who require evidence before renewal, protecting the $14.00 contribution per unit and helping justify the $1,200,000 line.

Disadvantage: The cameras and computing for optical inspection add to the $12.00 variable cost per unit at a time when semiconductor and servo-motor inputs have risen 14.2%, so the $1.20 premium may not cover the extra cost. The system also needs technicians with computer-vision skills, yet 15 of 62 lack them and turnover is rising; until they are trained, false alarms could slow the 9,800 cells assembled each quarter rather than speed them up. Inspecting every weld also creates large amounts of image data, which could extend the 4.1-day mean repair time and leave the 96.4% first-pass yield unchanged despite the $1,200,000 outlay.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to XPL's defect rate, survey data and skills.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in semiconductor and servo-motor costs will affect XPL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. The insert states $700,000 of hire purchase but not its rate terms, so the only defensible figure is a labelled bound: if that $700,000 were fully exposed to the move, the added annual cost would be 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250, small beside $420,000 of fixed costs. If the agreement is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero, and XPL can also reduce it by funding more from the $500,000 share issue.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, from $12.60 to $13.49): Each paid hour costs $0.895 more (7.1% × $12.60). The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; with 62 staff and rising technician turnover every replacement is hired at the higher rate. Productivity is 60,000 units ÷ 62 staff = about 968 units per worker, and if that falls, unit labour cost rises and the $14.00 contribution is squeezed while the 4.8% defect rate is being fixed.

Semiconductor and servo-motor costs (up 14.2%): These are direct inputs into the robots and the planned optical-inspection system, and 14.2% is by far the largest percentage change in the bulletin, more than double the wage rise and nineteen times the 0.75-point rate move. The insert gives no separate materials bill, so only the scale can be stated, but the cost lands on every one of the 60,000 units while automation demand grew only 4.8%, limiting XPL's ability to pass it on.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in semiconductor and servo-motor costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest shock, it is unavoidable for a robotics maker, and it hits all 60,000 units and the $1,200,000 line at once when demand grew only 4.8%. The wage rise is second because it recurs with each of the 62 staff, while the interest effect is smallest and can be avoided by fixing terms or using the share issue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to XPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on XPL's costs, finance or prices in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that component costs have the greatest impact and clear reasons why the other two are smaller.
